chief_complaint: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray and dry cough
hpi_details: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest x-ray and dry cough. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the cough is just a stubborn viral bug she picked up that won't go away, with the chest shadows being leftover mucus congestion.
concerns: She is worried that the enlarged spots in her chest mean she has lymphoma or chest cancer like her aunt died from.
expectations: She hopes to be referred for a CT scan or specialist evaluation to confirm whether the spots are cancerous.

available_results.value: Symmetric bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without focal consolidation

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Sarcoidosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of compatible findings after excluding infection, malignancy, and exposure-related disease; treatment is based on organ involvement and severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Sarcoidosis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Sarcoidosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Community-acquired pneumonia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90%).
management_principles: Assess pulmonary severity and screen for eye, skin, cardiac, neurologic, renal, and calcium-related involvement.
Refer for specialist-led confirmation and organ-specific management; corticosteroids require individualized clinician direction.
Escalate urgently for severe hypoxemia, respiratory distress, syncope, chest pain, visual loss, or sustained palpitations.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.objective: Dry cough and incidental imaging finding
must_ask.say: How long have you had this dry cough, and were you having any symptoms before the chest X-ray was done?
Have you had any skin rashes or bumps, eye redness or pain, or joint swelling?
Have you had fevers, night sweats, or unusual tiredness recently?

must_ask.objective: Occupational and environmental exposure to exclude mimics
must_ask.say: Have you worked with beryllium, or been exposed to birds, mould, or organic dusts?

must_ask.objective: Ethnicity and family history relevant to sarcoidosis risk
must_ask.say: Has anyone in your family had sarcoidosis or a similar granulomatous condition?

history.answer: I have had this dry cough that won't go away, and my routine health checkup chest X-ray showed enlarged lymph nodes in both lungs.
The cough started about four weeks ago and has been gradually getting more noticeable over time.
It didn't begin after a cold or flu, and I have never had an episode like this before.
It is completely dry with no phlegm, mucus, or foul odor at all.
I cough throughout the day, and it doesn't get noticeably worse at night, early morning, or when I lie down.
Nothing specific seems to trigger it; cold air, dust, and talking don't make it much worse.
No, they aren't severe coughing fits, there is no gasping or whooping sound, and I have never vomited from coughing.
I haven't heard any wheezing or whistling sounds, and I only feel slightly short of breath if I push myself hard during exercise.
No, I haven't had any fever or chills.
No, I have never coughed up blood or seen any blood specks.
I haven't had drenching night sweats or noticeable weight loss, though I have felt unusually tired.
I have been feeling generalized fatigue and low energy for the past few weeks.
No, I don't feel any chest pain, tightness, or pain when I take a deep breath.
No runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, or sensation of mucus dripping down the back of my throat.
No heartburn, sour fluid backing up into my mouth, or lump sensation in my throat.
No, I can sleep flat without getting short of breath, and my legs have not swollen.
My vision is completely normal, with no eye pain, redness, or sensitivity to light.
I haven't noticed any new skin rashes, red bumps on my shins, or unusual patches on my face.
No heart flutters, racing heartbeat, lightheadedness, or blacking out.
My joints feel fine, with no pain, stiffness, or history of kidney stones.
I had a routine health screening two weeks ago, and the doctor told me the X-ray showed enlarged lymph nodes on both sides of my lungs.
I thought it was just a lingering dry cough from a bad cold I couldn't shake off, maybe with some trapped congestion.
When they mentioned enlarged lymph nodes in my chest, I immediately panicked that it could be lymphoma or cancer like my aunt had.
No one at home or in my office has been sick or coughing.
I have never been exposed to anyone with tuberculosis, and I have never had a positive TB test or treatment.
I work at a desk in an office, and I have never been exposed to birds, mold, asbestos, silica, or metal dust like beryllium.
I do not have asthma, seasonal allergies, allergic rhinitis, or eczema.
I have never had high blood pressure and have never taken blood pressure medications or ACE inhibitors.
I have always been healthy and have no history of chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one glass of wine or beer once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager and live in an apartment with my husband and two children.
There is no family history of sarcoidosis, lung diseases, autoimmune conditions, or lymphoma.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 74 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air, temperature 36.7 C.
Nasal mucosa pink without edema or secretions; posterior oropharynx clear without erythema or cobblestoning.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Symmetric chest wall expansion with normal tactile fremitus and no tenderness to palpation.
Resonant percussion note heard symmetrically throughout both lung fields.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with vesicular breathing; no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Conjunctivae non-injected, sclerae anicteric, pupils equally round and reactive to light with no photophobia or redness.
No skin plaques, violaceous facial lesions, or tender erythematous nodules on the lower extremities.
No pretibial or ankle edema bilaterally; no digital clubbing or peripheral cyanosis.
